O P E R A T I O N A L S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y
Sustainable
Supply Chains
Integrating environmental considerations into sourcing, production, and distribution
01

You already know 70–90% of a company's footprint lives in its 
supply chain.
Today is about what to actually do about it.
Three stages — sourcing, production, distribution — and the specific interventions, standards, and case studies that 
make each one measurably more sustainable.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 02

Following the Product, Upstream to Downstream
Sustainable Supply Chain Management (SSCM): integrating environmental and social criteria into every decision along a product's journey — not just at the factory 
gate.
01
Sourcing
Where raw materials come from, and 
under what conditions.
02
Production
How materials become products — and 
at what environmental cost.
03
Distribution
How products move to market — often 
the most visible emissions of all.
04
Measuring the Chain
Mapping, tracking, and reporting the 
whole system end to end.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 04

S E C T I O N 1 O F 4
Sustainable Sourcing
Where raw materials come from, and under what conditions — the origin point of most supply chain risk.
05

S E C T I O N 1 · D E F I N I T I O N
What Is Sustainable Sourcing?
The furthest-upstream link in the chain — and, per the GHG Protocol, usually the largest share of a company's real footprint.
The Working Definition Procuring raw materials and components in ways that account for environmental impact, labor conditions, and 
long-term resource availability — not price alone.
Why Upstream Matters Most Categories 1 and 4 of Scope 3 (purchased goods, upstream transportation) are frequently a company's single 
largest emissions category — often larger than its own operations.
The Core Challenge A company rarely owns its suppliers — sustainable sourcing means influencing behavior it cannot directly 
control, several tiers removed from its own operations.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 06

S C O P E 3 : C a t e g o r i e s :
Upstream Scope 3 — Categories 1 to 8
Everything that happens before a product or service reaches your organization.
1. Purchased Goods & Services
Emissions from producing everything your 
organization buys or acquires.
2. Capital Goods
Emissions from producing purchased long￾term assets — machinery, buildings, 
equipment.
3. Fuel- & Energy-Related Activities
Upstream emissions of fuel and energy not 
already counted in Scope 1 or 2.
4. Upstream Transportation & 
Distribution
Third-party transport of purchased products 
to your organization.
5. Waste Generated in Operations
Emissions from third-party disposal and 
treatment of your operational waste.
6. Business Travel
Employee travel for business in vehicles not 
owned by the organization — flights, trains, 
taxis.
7. Employee Commuting
Emissions from employees' travel between 
home and work.
8. Upstream Leased Assets
Emissions from operating assets you lease, 
not already in Scope 1 or 2.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 28

S E C T I O N 1 · W H A T C A N G O W R O N G
Four Categories of Sourcing Risk
The specific failure modes that make upstream sourcing the riskiest link in most supply chains.
Deforestation-Linked 
Commodities
Palm oil, soy, cattle, and timber are 
consistently linked to tropical 
deforestation when sourced without 
traceability.
Conflict Minerals
Tin, tungsten, tantalum, and gold 
sourced from conflict-affected regions 
can finance armed groups and human 
rights abuses.
Forced & Child Labour
Complex, multi-tier supply chains can 
obscure labor abuses far removed from 
the buying company's direct view.
Biodiversity & Habitat Loss
Extraction of raw materials — mining, 
fishing, logging — can degrade 
ecosystems far from where the final 
product is sold.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 07

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E R E S P O N S E
Certifications That Address Sourcing Risk
Third-party certification is the primary tool buyers use to verify claims they cannot check themselves.
Fairtrade
Certifies fair prices and labor standards 
for commodities like coffee, cocoa, and 
cotton, verified by independent audit.
Forest Stewardship Council (FSC)
Certifies wood and paper products from 
responsibly managed forests, with full 
chain-of-custody tracking.
Rainforest Alliance
Certifies farms meeting environmental, 
social, and economic sustainability 
criteria, common in coffee, tea, and 
cocoa.
Responsible Minerals Initiative
Audits smelters and refiners to verify 
minerals are not sourced from conflict￾affected or high-risk areas.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 08

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
When Sourcing Oversight Fails: Rana Plaza
The Rana Plaza Collapse, Dhaka, Bangladesh (April 24, 2013)
An eight-story building housing five garment factories collapsed, killing 1,134 workers and injuring approximately 2,500 more — the deadliest disaster in the 
history of the garment industry.
The Sourcing Failure
The factories supplied major global apparel brands, whose supplier audits had never 
identified the building's fundamental structural defects.
The Warning Ignored
Visible cracks were discovered the day before the collapse; workers were ordered back to 
their 13–14 hour shifts regardless.
The Systemic Response
The legally binding Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh was signed within a 
month by over 200 global brands and retailers.
The Lesson
Supplier audits that check labor and quality standards, but not structural safety, can miss 
the most catastrophic risks entirely.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 09

◆ INTERACTIVE T H I N K & S H A R E
"A brand's supplier audit checks fire exits and pay 
stubs, but not structural engineering. What other 
kinds of 'invisible' risk might a standard audit 
checklist miss today?"
Think beyond garments — electronics, food, minerals.

SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 10

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
For most companies, which GHG Protocol Scope 3 categories are 
most directly addressed by sustainable sourcing practices?
A Category 11 (Use of sold products) and Category 12 (End-of-life)
B Category 1 (Purchased goods & services) and Category 4 (Upstream transportation)
C Category 6 (Business travel) only
D Sourcing has no connection to Scope 3 at all
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. Category 1 (Purchased goods & services) 
and Category 4 (Upstream transportation)
Sustainable sourcing addresses the upstream 
categories of Scope 3 most directly — Category 1 
(purchased goods & services) and Category 4 
(upstream transportation) — which are frequently a 
company's single largest emissions categories.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 11

S E C T I O N 2 O F 4
Sustainable Production
How raw materials become products — and the environmental cost embedded in every design choice.
12

S E C T I O N 2 · D E F I N I T I O N
What Is Sustainable Production?
Manufacturing that minimizes environmental impact per unit of output — not simply "cleaner factories."
The Working Definition Producing goods using processes and materials that minimize energy use, water use, waste, and toxic emissions 
relative to the value created.
Cleaner Production, Not End-of-Pipe The modern approach prevents pollution and waste at the source — in process and material design — rather 
than treating waste after it's already created.
Why It's a Design Problem The vast majority of a product's environmental impact is locked in at the design stage, long before a single unit is 
manufactured.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 13

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E C O R E T O O L
Life Cycle Assessment (LCA)
The standardized method for actually measuring a product's environmental impact — from raw material to disposal.
Cradle-to-Gate Measures impact from raw material extraction through to the factory gate — the boundary most manufacturers 
can measure directly.
Cradle-to-Grave Extends the assessment through use and disposal — the full picture of a product's lifetime impact.
Cradle-to-Cradle Extends further still: designed explicitly so the product's materials become the raw material for the next product 
cycle.
Why It Matters Here LCA is what lets a company compare two production or material choices quantitatively, instead of guessing 
which is "greener."
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 14

S E C T I O N 2 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Comparing Packaging Materials with LCA Thinking
G I V E N
Two packaging options, each weighing 50 g (0.050 kg) per unit
Option A — Virgin plastic: embodied emissions of 3.5 kgCO₂e per kg of 
material produced
Option B — Recycled plastic (rPET): embodied emissions of 1.2 kgCO₂e per kg 
of material produced
F O R M U L A
Embodied Emissions per Unit = Weight (kg) × Emission Factor 
(kgCO₂e/kg)
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Option A: 0.050 kg × 3.5 kgCO₂e/kg = 0.175 kgCO₂e per unit
2 Option B: 0.050 kg × 1.2 kgCO₂e/kg = 0.060 kgCO₂e per unit
3 Savings per unit: 0.175 − 0.060 = 0.115 kgCO₂e
4 At 1 million units produced per year: 0.115 kg × 1,000,000 = 115,000 kg = 115 tonnes CO₂e saved
115 t CO₂e / Year A single material substitution — virgin to recycled plastic — saves the equivalent of many households' annual emissions, without
changing the product itself.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 15

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E T O O L K I T
Four Cleaner Production Techniques
Concrete interventions that reduce environmental impact at the point of manufacture.
Energy & Water Efficiency
Optimizing industrial processes to use 
less energy and water per unit of output 
— often the fastest payback in a factory.
Waste Minimization
Redesigning processes to generate less 
scrap, off-cuts, and by-product in the 
first place — not just recycling more of it.
Safer Chemical Substitution
Replacing hazardous solvents, dyes, and 
inputs with less toxic alternatives that 
achieve the same manufacturing result.
Process Optimization
Fine-tuning temperatures, cycle times, 
and equipment settings to cut energy 
and material use without changing the 
product.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 16

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
What is the key difference between "cradle-to-gate" and "cradle-to￾cradle" in Life Cycle Assessment?
A They measure exactly the same boundary
B
Cradle-to-gate stops at the factory; cradle-to-cradle is designed so end-of-life materials 
become new raw material
C Cradle-to-cradle only applies to food products
D Cradle-to-gate includes disposal, cradle-to-cradle does not
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. Cradle-to-gate stops at the factory; 
cradle-to-cradle is designed so end-of-life 
materials become new raw material
Cradle-to-gate measures impact only up to the factory 
gate. Cradle-to-cradle is the most ambitious boundary 
— the product and its materials are explicitly designed 
to become the raw material for a future product cycle, 
embodying circular economy principles directly in the 
LCA scope.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 17

S E C T I O N 3 O F 4
Sustainable Distribution
How products move to market — often the most visible, and most easily reducible, link in the chain.
18

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E S C A L E O F T H E P R O B L E M
Distribution's Environmental Footprint
~1/5
Share of global CO₂ emissions attributable to the 
transport sector as a whole
4–6
Category 4 (upstream) and Category 9 (downstream) 
transportation — two of the most under-measured 
Scope 3 categories
75×
How much more emissions-intensive air freight is than 
sea freight, for the same cargo and distance
Distribution choices are unusual in sustainability: the lowest-carbon option is frequently also the lowest-cost option — a rare true win-win.
Source: Illustrative figures based on published freight-transport emission factors (e.g., DEFRA, ICCT).
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 19

S E C T I O N 3 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Comparing Freight Transport Modes
G I V E N
Shipment: 20 tonnes of goods, travelling 6,000 km
Sea freight emission factor: ~10 gCO₂e per tonne-km
Air freight emission factor: ~600 gCO₂e per tonne-km
F O R M U L A
Emissions (kg) = Weight (t) × Distance (km) × Emission Factor 
(g/t·km) ÷ 1,000
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Sea freight: 20 × 6,000 × 10 ÷ 1,000 = 1,200 kg ≈ 1.2 tonnes CO₂e
2 Air freight: 20 × 6,000 × 600 ÷ 1,000 = 72,000 kg = 72 tonnes CO₂e
3 Ratio: 72 ÷ 1.2 = 60× more emissions for the identical shipment, moved by air instead of sea
60× Difference The mode choice alone — sea versus air, for the exact same cargo — changes the shipment's footprint by a factor of 60. Mode 
shift is one of the highest-leverage decisions in distribution.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 20

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E T O O L K I T
Five Levers of Sustainable Distribution
Interventions that reduce distribution's footprint without necessarily changing what is sold.
Modal Shift
Moving freight from air or 
road to sea or rail wherever 
transit time allows — the 
single highest-leverage lever 
available.
Route Optimization
Software-driven routing that 
reduces total distance 
travelled and empty return 
trips ("deadheading").
Packaging Reduction
Lighter, right-sized packaging 
reduces both material use and 
the weight (and therefore 
fuel) needed to ship it.
Warehouse Efficiency
Locating distribution centers 
closer to demand, and using 
energy-efficient warehouse 
operations, cuts both distance 
and energy use.
Reverse Logistics
Efficient systems for returns, 
repairs, and end-of-life 
collection keep products and 
materials circulating rather 
than being discarded.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 21

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
In the worked example, why did the air freight shipment produce 
roughly 60 times more emissions than the identical sea freight 
shipment?
A The air shipment travelled a much longer distance
B The air shipment carried more weight
C Air freight has a much higher emission factor (gCO₂e per tonne-km) than sea freight
D There is no real difference between air and sea freight emissions
A N S W E R & W H Y
C. Air freight has a much higher emission 
factor (gCO₂e per tonne-km) than sea 
freight
Both shipments had identical weight and distance —
the entire 60× difference comes from the emission 
factor itself: air freight emits far more CO₂e per tonne￾kilometre than sea freight, due to the energy intensity 
of air transport.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 23

S E C T I O N 4 O F 4
Measuring & Managing the Chain
You cannot manage what you cannot see — the visibility problem underneath every claim in this lecture.
24

S E C T I O N 4 · T H E V I S I B I L I T Y P R O B L E M
Supply Chain Tiers: Why Visibility Collapses Fast
Most companies can see their direct suppliers clearly — and almost nothing beyond that.
Tier 1
Direct suppliers the company contracts with and 
pays directly.
Usually well audited and visible.
Tier 2
Suppliers to your Tier 1 suppliers — e.g., the fabric 
mill supplying a garment factory.
Visibility drops sharply here.
Tier 3+
Raw material extraction — mines, farms, forests —
often multiple contractual layers removed.
Frequently invisible to the buying company entirely.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 25

S E C T I O N 4 · C O N N E C T I N G B A C K
The Whole Lecture Is a Scope 3 Map
Every stage covered today maps directly onto specific GHG Protocol Scope 3 categories.
Sourcing Cat. 1 — Purchased goods & services · Cat. 2 — Capital goods
Production Cat. 3 — Fuel- & energy-related activities · Cat. 5 — Waste generated in operations
Distribution Cat. 4 — Upstream transportation · Cat. 9 — Downstream transportation
End-of-Life (Beyond Today) Cat. 11 — Use of sold products · Cat. 12 — End-of-life treatment
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 26

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
When Supplier Engagement Works at Scale: Project Gigaton
Walmart's Project Gigaton (Launched 2017)
Walmart invited its more than 100,000 suppliers to voluntarily reduce or avoid 1 billion metric tons (a gigaton) of greenhouse gas emissions from its supply chain by 2030 
— targeting energy, waste, packaging, transportation, nature, and product design.
The Result
In February 2024, Walmart announced suppliers had collectively reported over 1 billion metric 
tons reduced or avoided — six years ahead of the 2030 target.
The Scale
More than 5,000 suppliers ultimately participated — described as one of the largest private￾sector supply chain sustainability consortia ever assembled.
The Method
Not top-down mandates — a shared toolkit, education, financing support, and public 
recognition for supplier progress.
The Honest Caveat
The same year, Walmart disclosed its own direct (Scope 1 & 2) operational emissions rose 3.9% 
— supply chain success and operational progress are not the same thing.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 27

S E C T I O N 4 · C L O S I N G T H E V I S I B I L I T Y G A P
Technology for Supply Chain Traceability
The engineering opportunity underneath everything in this lecture — visibility itself is a data problem.
Blockchain-Based Traceability Distributed ledgers can record a product's custody chain immutably, from raw material to shelf, making origin 
claims independently verifiable.
Satellite & Remote Sensing Monitoring platforms can detect deforestation or land-use change linked to specific supply chain regions in near 
real time.
Supplier Data Platforms Software that aggregates supplier-reported emissions, labor, and safety data into a single auditable system, 
replacing scattered spreadsheets.
Why This Is Your Opportunity Every technology on this slide is still immature relative to the scale of the problem — this is one of the most 
under-built areas in all of climate tech.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 28

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
Why does supply chain visibility typically collapse beyond Tier 1 
suppliers?
A Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers are always located in different countries
B
Companies have direct contracts only with Tier 1 suppliers, and visibility depends on those 
suppliers disclosing their own suppliers in turn
C Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers are legally required to remain anonymous
D Visibility does not actually decrease at any tier
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. Companies have direct contracts only 
with Tier 1 suppliers, and visibility depends 
on those suppliers disclosing their own 
suppliers in turn
A company's direct contractual relationship is with its 
Tier 1 suppliers. Seeing further upstream requires 
those suppliers to voluntarily disclose their own 
suppliers — a chain of disclosure that gets weaker, 
and less enforceable, at every additional tier.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 29

B R I N G I N G I T T O G E T H E R
One Chain, Three Interventions, One Measurement System
Sourcing, production, and distribution are not separate sustainability projects — they are three points on the same value chain, measured by the same framework.
Sustainable Sourcing Reduces risk and impact before a material ever enters the factory — certifications and audits are the tools.
Sustainable Production Reduces impact per unit made — Life Cycle Assessment is the tool that makes design choices comparable.
Sustainable Distribution Reduces impact per unit moved — mode shift is the single highest-leverage lever available.
Measurement & Visibility Ties all three together into one Scope 3 inventory — and is the actual bottleneck most companies face today.
SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 30

◆ INTERACTIVE A P P L Y I T A L L
"Pick a product you own. Trace it backward: 
where was it sourced, produced, and distributed 
from — and which of today's three interventions 
would improve it most?"
This is exactly how a real supply chain sustainability audit begins.

SUST AI N AB LE SUP P LY CH AI N S 32

O P E R A T I O N A L S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y
Resource
Management
Energy Efficiency · Water Conservation · Waste Reduction · Circular Economy Principles
01

The global economy is only 6.9% circular.
The other 93% is resources used once, then lost.
Today is entirely practical: the actual calculations engineers and facility managers use to cut energy, water, and waste 
— and the systems-level thinking that ties them together.
R E SOUR CE MAN AGE ME N T 02

T O D A Y ' S J O U R N E Y
Four Resources, One Systems Problem
01
Energy Efficiency
Doing the same work with less power —
and calculating whether it pays for itself.
02
Water Conservation
Protecting the resource India is running 
out of fastest.
03
Waste Reduction
The hierarchy of what to do with 
material before it becomes garbage.
04
The Circular Economy
The systems-level model that ties all 
three together permanently.
R E SOUR CE MAN AGE ME N T 04

S E C T I O N 1 O F 4
Energy Efficiency
Delivering the same output, service, or comfort — while using measurably less power.
05

S E C T I O N 1 · D E F I N I T I O N
What Is Energy Efficiency?
A precise engineering concept, often confused with its cousin, energy conservation.
The Working Definition Using less energy to provide the same product, service, or level of comfort — doing the same job, with less 
input.
Efficiency vs. Conservation Conservation reduces energy use by reducing the service itself (turning off a light); efficiency reduces energy use 
while keeping the service the same (a more efficient light, on for the same hours).
Energy Intensity: The Macro View Energy used per unit of economic output (e.g., MJ per unit of GDP) — a country-level indicator of how efficiently 
an economy converts energy into value.
R E SOUR CE MAN AGE ME N T 06

S E C T I O N 1 · W H E R E I T P A Y S O F F
Four Levers of Energy Efficiency
The same underlying logic — do more with less — applied across every major energy-consuming system.
Buildings & HVAC
Insulation, smart thermostats, and 
efficient heating/cooling — buildings 
account for a large share of global energy 
demand.
Industrial Processes
Waste heat recovery, efficient motors, 
and process optimization — often the 
fastest payback in an industrial facility.
Lighting
LED lighting uses a small fraction of the 
energy of incandescent bulbs for the 
same brightness — one of the simplest, 
fastest wins available.
Transport & Logistics
Fuel efficiency standards, route 
optimization, and electrification reduce 
energy use per kilometre travelled.
R E SOUR CE MAN AGE ME N T 07

S E C T I O N 1 · M A K I N G I T S Y S T E M A T I C
ISO 50001: Energy Management Systems
Efficiency gains stick when they're built into a management system — not left to one-off projects.
What It Is The international standard for establishing, implementing, and continually improving an energy management 
system within an organization.
The Core Cycle A Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle: set an energy baseline and targets, implement improvements, measure results, and 
adjust — repeated continuously.
Why It Matters It turns "we should save energy" into an auditable, repeatable organizational process — the same logic industrial 
quality systems use for defects.
R E SOUR CE MAN AGE ME N T 08

S E C T I O N 1 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Payback Period on an LED Lighting Retrofit
G I V E N
200 incandescent bulbs (60 W each), operating 10 hours/day
Replacing with 200 LED bulbs (9 W each)
Electricity cost: ₹7/kWh; Retrofit cost: ₹250/bulb (₹50,000 total)
F O R M U L A
Payback Period (years) = Total Investment ÷ Annual Cost Savings
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Power saved per bulb: 60W − 9W = 51W = 0.051 kW
2 Daily savings (200 bulbs): 0.051 kW × 10 hrs × 200 = 102 kWh/day → 37,230 kWh/year
3 Annual cost savings: 37,230 kWh × ₹7/kWh = ₹2,60,610/year
4 Payback: ₹50,000 ÷ ₹2,60,610 ≈ 0.19 years ≈ 2.3 months
≈ 2.3 Months The retrofit pays for itself in under three months — incandescent-to-LED conversions are among the fastest-payback efficiency 
investments that exist.
R E SOUR CE MAN AGE ME N T 09

◆ INTERACTIVE T H I N K & S H A R E
"Of the four levers — buildings, industry, lighting, 
transport — which do you think offers the fastest 
payback for a typical Indian college campus, and 
why?"
Think about what's cheapest to retrofit versus what saves the most energy.

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
What is the key difference between energy efficiency and energy 
conservation?
A They are exactly the same thing
B
Efficiency keeps the service the same while using less energy; conservation reduces the 
service itself
C Conservation only applies to industry, efficiency only to buildings
D Efficiency always costs more than conservation
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. Efficiency keeps the service the same 
while using less energy; conservation 
reduces the service itself
Energy conservation reduces energy use by reducing 
or eliminating the service (e.g., turning off a light). 
Energy efficiency reduces energy use while keeping 
the exact same service level (e.g., a more efficient 
light, on for the same number of hours) — a subtle but 
important engineering distinction.
R E SOUR CE MAN AGE ME N T 11

S E C T I O N 2 O F 4
Water Conservation
Protecting the resource that India, specifically, is running out of fastest.
12

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E U R G E N C Y
India's Water Stress, By The Numbers
~600 M
Indians facing high to extreme water 
stress (NITI Aayog, CWMI)
820 M
People live in river basins with per 
capita availability at or below the 
scarcity threshold
1,486 m³
India's per capita water availability 
(2021), projected to fall toward 1,140 
m³ by 2050
18% / 4%
Share of world's population India 
holds, versus share of world's 
freshwater resources
India's water demand is projected to be twice its available supply by 2030 — an estimated 6% loss of GDP if unaddressed.

R E SOUR CE MAN AGE ME N T 13

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E T O O L K I T
Four Tools for Water Conservation
Interventions available at every scale, from a single building to an entire watershed.
Low-Flow Fixtures
Efficient taps, showerheads, and dual￾flush toilets can cut household and 
institutional water use significantly with 
no change in service.
Rainwater Harvesting
Capturing rooftop and surface runoff for 
direct use or groundwater recharge —
cheap, decentralized, and highly 
effective at scale.
Wastewater Recycling
Treating and reusing greywater and 
treated sewage for irrigation, cooling, or 
flushing — reducing demand on 
freshwater sources.
Precision Irrigation
Drip and micro-irrigation target water

agriculture consumes roughly 85% of

Calculating Rainwater Harvesting Potential
G I V E N
Rooftop catchment area: 500 m²
Average annual rainfall in the region: 900 mm (0.9 m)
Runoff coefficient for a concrete roof: 0.85 (85% collection efficiency)
F O R M U L A
Harvestable Water (litres) = Area (m²) × Rainfall (m) × Runoff 
Coefficient × 1000
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Volume of rain falling on the roof: 500 m² × 0.9 m = 450 m³
2 Apply the runoff coefficient: 450 m³ × 0.85 = 382.5 m³
3 Convert to litres: 382.5 × 1,000 = 3,82,500 litres
3.83 Lakh L/Year This single rooftop can realistically harvest nearly 4 lakh litres of water annually — enough to meaningfully offset a building's 
freshwater demand.

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E C O R E F R A M E W O R K
The Waste Hierarchy
Not all waste management options are equal — this hierarchy ranks them from most to least preferred.
1. Refuse & Reduce Avoid creating the waste in the first place — the only tier that eliminates impact entirely.
2. Reuse Use a product again, in its original form, for the same or a different purpose.
3. Recycle Break a material down and remanufacture it into something new.
4. Recover Extract energy from waste that cannot be reused or recycled (e.g., waste-to-energy).
5. Dispose Landfill — the least preferred option, used only when nothing else is possible.

S E C T I O N 3 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Calculating a City's Landfill Diversion Rate
G I V E N
A city generates 1,000 tonnes of municipal solid waste per day
Of this: 350 tonnes is composted, 150 tonnes is recycled
The remaining 500 tonnes goes to landfill
F O R M U L A
Diversion Rate (%) = (Waste Diverted from Landfill ÷ Total Waste 
Generated) × 100
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Total waste diverted: composted + recycled = 350 + 150 = 500 tonnes
2 Diversion rate: (500 ÷ 1,000) × 100 = 50%
50% Diversion Exactly half of this city's waste is being kept out of the landfill — the standard metric cities and campuses use to track waste
management progress.

S E C T I O N 3 · W H O P A Y S F O R E N D - OF - L I F E
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)
A policy principle that shifts the cost and responsibility for waste back onto the companies that created it.
The Core Idea Producers are made financially and physically responsible for the end-of-life management of the products and 
packaging they place on the market.
India's E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 Mandate producers of electronics to meet specific e-waste collection and recycling targets, obtained through 
registered recyclers.
India's Plastic Waste Management Rules Require producers, importers, and brand owners of plastic packaging to meet EPR targets for collection and 
recycling.
Why It Changes Behaviour When producers bear disposal costs, they have a direct financial incentive to design products that are easier and 
cheaper to recycle.

The Circular Economy
The systems-level model that ties energy, water, and waste together — permanently, not as separate projects.

S E C T I O N 4 · T H E F R A M E W O R K
Three Principles of a Circular Economy
As defined by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation — the most widely cited framework in the field.
Design Out Waste & Pollution Waste is treated as a design flaw, not an inevitability — products and systems are designed from the outset to 
prevent it.
Keep Products & Materials in Use Through reuse, repair, remanufacturing, and recycling — extending value for as long as physically possible.
Regenerate Natural Systems Circular systems actively rebuild natural capital — returning nutrients to soil, restoring ecosystems — not just 
minimizing harm.

S E C T I O N 4 · T W O K I N D S O F C I R C U L A T I O N
The Technical Cycle vs. the Biological Cycle
The Ellen MacArthur Foundation's "butterfly diagram" splits circularity into two distinct loops, based on what kind of material is involved.
The Technical Cycle
Applies to durable, manufactured materials: metals, plastics, glass, electronics.
Circulates through maintenance, reuse, refurbishment, remanufacturing, and 
recycling.
Goal: keep the material in a manufactured loop indefinitely, never returning to 
raw extraction.
The Biological Cycle
Applies to renewable, biodegradable materials: food waste, natural fibers, 
wood.
Circulates through composting and anaerobic digestion, safely returning 
nutrients to the soil.
Goal: regenerate natural systems, not just avoid landfill.

B R I N G I N G I T T O G E T H E R
One Systems Problem, Not Four Separate Ones
Energy, water, and waste are not independent projects — the circular economy is the framework that shows why.
Energy Efficiency Reduces the energy embedded in every material extracted, processed, and moved — the "energy losses" pathway in the Value 
Gap.
Water Conservation Recycled water and precision irrigation are themselves circular loops — keeping a resource in use instead of extracting more.
Waste Reduction The waste hierarchy is a miniature version of the circular economy — refuse and reuse before recycle, recycle before dispose.
The Circular Economy The framework that shows these three are not separate initiatives — they are one system, viewed from three different points.
